claim: Barriers to microbial migrations can lead to adaptive radiations and increased endemism.
source: Barriers to microbial migrations can lead adaptive radiations and increased endemism.
evidence: This is a general theoretical statement presented in the abstract without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Extreme unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry of essential nutrients can be a barrier to microbial immigration over geological timescales.
source: We propose that extreme unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry of essential nutrients can be a barrier to microbial immigration over geological timescales.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations and reasoning.

claim: At the oasis in the Cuatro Ciénegas Basin in Mexico, nutrient stoichiometric proportions are skewed given the low phosphorus availability in the ecosystem.
source: At the oasis in the Cuatro Ciénegas Basin in Mexico, nutrient stoichiometric proportions are skewed given the low phosphorus availability in the ecosystem.
evidence: This statement is supported by data presented in the manuscript about nutrient measurements.

claim: The ancient niche of extreme unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry favoured survival of ancestral microorganisms.
source: The ancient niche of extreme unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry favoured survival of ancestral microorganisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic and ecological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Extreme nutrient imbalance persisted due to environmental stability and low extinction rates, generating a diverse and unique bacterial community.
source: This extreme nutrient imbalance persisted due to environmental stability and low extinction rates, generating a diverse and unique bacterial community.
evidence: This is supported by diversification rate analyses and diversity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Several endemic clades of Bacillus invaded the Cuatro Cienegas region in two geological times, the late Precambrian and the Jurassic.
source: Several endemic clades of Bacillus invaded the Cuatro Cienegas region in two geological times, the late Precambrian and the Jurassic.
evidence: This is supported by molecular clock analyses and phylogenetic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Other lineages of Bacillus, Clostridium and Bacteroidetes migrated into the basin in isolated events.
source: Other lineages of Bacillus, Clostridium and Bacteroidetes migrated into the basin in isolated events.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analyses showing non-monophyletic groups.

claim: Organized forms of life like microbial mats and stromatolites were dominant for billions of years during the Proterozoic.
source: Scientists have looked for analogs of such worlds in environments possessing living microbial mats and stromatolites, since these organized forms of life were dominant for billions of years during the Proterozoic (Nutman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nutman et al., 2017.

claim: Most contemporary stromatolite and microbial mat communities contain mostly contemporary microbial lineages rather than ancient ones.
source: Nevertheless, in most cases these communities represent more a physical metaphor of the past than an actual lost world, since they contain mostly contemporary microbial lineages (White et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to White et al., 2015 and Wong et al., 2015.

claim: The Cuatro Ciénegas Basin contains abundant and morphologically diverse stromatolites and microbial mats.
source: The exception seems to be the abundant and morphologically diverse stromatolites and microbial mats found in the endangered oasis of Cuatro Ciénegas Basin (CCB) in Northern Mexico.
evidence: This is a direct observation reported by the authors.

claim: The Cuatro Ciénegas Basin is an extremely diverse wetland.
source: In this extremely diverse wetland (Minckley, 1969), the recycling of the deep aquifer by magmatic heat replicates many conditions of ancient oceans (Wolaver et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Minckley, 1969 and Wolaver et al., 2013.

claim: The recycling of the deep aquifer by magmatic heat in CCB replicates many conditions of ancient oceans.
source: the recycling of the deep aquifer by magmatic heat replicates many conditions of ancient oceans (Wolaver et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wolaver et al., 2013.

claim: CCB has extremely unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry.
source: including its extremely unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry (Elser et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Elser et al., 2006.

claim: CCB has sulphur and magnesium minerals that replicate marine osmolarity despite being low in NaCl.
source: and sulphur and magnesium minerals that replicate marine osmolarity (Wolaver et al., 2013; De Anda et al., 2017; Rebollar et al., 2012), despite being low in NaCl.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wolaver et al., 2013; De Anda et al., 2017; Rebollar et al., 2012.

claim: Isotopic analysis suggests that the deep aquifer maintained the ancestral marine conditions in the wetland by dissolving the existing minerals from its sediments.
source: Moreover, isotopic analysis suggests that the deep aquifer maintained the ancestral marine conditions in the wetland by dissolving the existing minerals from its sediments (Wolaver et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wolaver et al., 2013.

claim: A 16:1 nitrogen to phosphorus ratio (the Redfield ratio) is common to most life on Earth.
source: Ecological analyses have revealed that a 16:1 nitrogen to phosphorus (the Redfield ratio) is common to most life on Earth (Elser et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Elser et al., 2006.

claim: Ancient marine bacteria and hydrothermal vent-associated sulphur microbes survive in the CCB oasis.
source: We believe that these niche variables can explain the survival in this oasis of ancient marine bacteria and hydrothermal vent-associated sulphur microbes (Souza et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Souza et al., 2006.

claim: Marine microbes have stayed at CCB for hundreds of millions of years since this site was on the coasts of Laurentia for a very long time.
source: Our hypothesis is that such marine microbes have stayed there for hundreds of millions of years (Torsvik, 2003), since this site was on the coasts of Laurentia for a very long time.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to Torsvik, 2003.

claim: The uplifts of the Sierras isolated CCB from the Western Seaway 35 million years ago.
source: This changed 35 mya, with the uplifts of the Sierras that isolated CCB from the Western Seaway (Souza et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Souza et al., 2006.

claim: The aridification of the Chihuahuan desert occurred in the last 7 million years.
source: and the aridification of the Chihuahuan desert in the last 7 million years.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on geological knowledge.

claim: Viral metagenomics revealed substantial divergence of CCB viruses from continental waters and a strong similarity with those of marine habitats.
source: In this 'lost world', even the most dynamic part of the community, the viruses, have maintained a marine signature, as viral metagenomics revealed substantial divergence of viruses from continental waters and a strong similarity with those of marine habitats (Desnues et al., 2008; Taboada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Desnues et al., 2008 and Taboada et al., 2018.

claim: There is a very high ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus (167:1) in the sediment of the Churince hydrological system.
source: There is a very high ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus (167:1) in the sediment of the Churince hydrological system, where most of the Bacillus of this study were sampled (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2017.

claim: Many CCB bacterial lineages show extreme imbalance at the bacterial intracellular level, with the most extreme being a nitrogen to phosphorus ratio of 965:1 in a strain of CCB Bacillus cereus group.
source: We see an imprint of this evolutionary history in the extreme imbalance at the bacterial intracellular level in many lineages (the most extreme being nitrogen to phosphorus ratio of 965:1 in a strain of CCB Bacillus cereus group) (Valdivia-Anistro et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Valdivia-Anistro et al., 2015.

claim: Some CCB Bacillus species can synthesize membrane sulfolipids, which appears to be an ancestral adaptation to limited phosphorus availability acquired from cyanobacteria by horizontal gene transfer.
source: and in the capability of some CCB Bacillus species to synthesize membrane sulfolipids, in what appears to be an ancestral adaptation to limited phosphorus availability acquired a long time ago from cyanobacteria by horizontal gene transfer (Alcaraz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alcaraz et al., 2008.

claim: Extreme unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry and rich sulphur conditions are niche characteristics of the Precambrian ocean that ended abruptly at the onset of the Phanerozoic Eon 542 mya with the weathering of continental apatite as consequence of several glaciation events.
source: Extreme unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry, as well as rich sulphur conditions, are niche characteristics of the Precambrian ocean, that ended abruptly at the onset of the Phanerozoic Eon 542 mya with the weathering of continental apatite as consequence of several glaciation events (Planavsky et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Planavsky et al., 2010.

claim: Molecular clock studies have suggested that some strains of culturable cyanobacteria from CCB diverged from their close relatives in the late Precambrian.
source: Moreover, using conservative time estimates based on geological events, molecular clock studies have suggested that some strains of culturable cyanobacteria (Domínguez-Escobar et al., 2011) as well as of Bacillus (Moreno-Letelier et al., 2012) from CCB diverged also from their close relatives in the late Precambrian.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Domínguez-Escobar et al., 2011 and Moreno-Letelier et al., 2012.

claim: Molecular clock studies have suggested that some strains of Bacillus from CCB diverged from their close relatives in the late Precambrian.
source: Moreover, using conservative time estimates based on geological events, molecular clock studies have suggested that some strains of culturable cyanobacteria (Domínguez-Escobar et al., 2011) as well as of Bacillus (Moreno-Letelier et al., 2012) from CCB diverged also from their close relatives in the late Precambrian.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moreno-Letelier et al., 2012.

claim: Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis are cosmopolitan bacteria with enormous population sizes and considerable migration rates.
source: We can observe this to apply for cosmopolitan bacteria, such as Escherichia coli or Bacillus subtilis, since these microbes have an enormous population size and considerable migration rates (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about these bacterial species.

claim: Isolation by distance has been observed for the thermophile Crenarchaeota Sulfolobus islandicus.
source: This isolation has been observed for the thermophile Crenarchaeota Sulfolobus islandicus (Reno et al., 2009) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reno et al., 2009.

claim: The island model of localized adaptation and rare migration occurs in microbes in the lakes in the Pyrenees, explained by the island-like nature of each lake.
source: This pattern also occurs in microbes, as is the case for those in the lakes in the Pyrenees, explained by the island-like nature of each lake (Casamayor, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Casamayor, 2017.

claim: A lost world would be both a physical space and a refugia, where communities survive in relictual conditions.
source: A lost world would be both a physical space and a refugia, where communities survive in relictual conditions.
evidence: This is a definition proposed by the authors.

claim: One signature for a lost world would be the presence of very deep phylogenetic branches, given that the time since isolation would be expected to be very long and extinctions rare.
source: One signature for a lost world would be the presence of very deep phylogenetic branches, given that the time since isolation would be expected to be very long and extinctions rare.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction made by the authors.

claim: Another signature for a lost world would be extreme niche conservatism by strong environmental filtering given the extremely unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry.
source: The other would be extreme niche conservatism, in this case by strong environmental filtering given the extremely unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction made by the authors.

claim: Churince is a closed hydrological system that depends on recharge by the deep aquifer contained in the Sierra San Marcos.
source: Churince is a closed hydrological system (and the most endangered site within CCB) and depends on recharge by the deep aquifer contained in the Sierra San Marcos (Wolaver et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wolaver et al., 2013.

claim: The Churince system used to consist of a spring, an intermediate lagoon and a large desiccation lagoon connected by a river.
source: The system used to consist of a spring, an intermediate lagoon and a large desiccation lagoon connected by a river (Minckley, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Minckley, 1969.

claim: By the time the microbial biodiversity was surveyed, the desiccation lagoon had already disappeared.
source: By the time we surveyed its microbial biodiversity, the desiccation lagoon had already disappeared.
evidence: This is a direct observation by the authors.

claim: The Churince's total Bacteria and Archaea richness is represented by a total of 5,167 OTUs assigned to samples from the water column, aquatic sediments, and soil.
source: The Churince's total Bacteria and Archaea richness is represented by a total of 5,167 OTUs assigned to samples from the water column, aquatic sediments, and soil.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data obtained by the authors.

claim: The assigned OTUs represented 60 different known phyla, three of which were Archaea.
source: These assigned OTUs represented 60 different known phyla, three of which were Archaea.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data obtained by the authors.

claim: Each site in Churince seems to have a unique taxonomic 'fingerprint' despite their spatial closeness.
source: Even though each site seems to have a unique taxonomic 'fingerprint' (Figure 3), despite their spatial closeness
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Aquatic sites in Churince share general patterns such as predominance of Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, and Bacteroidetes.
source: we also observed general patterns that aquatic sites share, such as predominance of Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, and Bacteroidetes.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data obtained by the authors.

claim: Sediments and soils in Churince are much more diverse than water sites and have important phyla in larger proportions than water sites, such as Firmicutes and Cyanobacteria.
source: Sediments and soils are much more diverse, and have important phyla in larger proportions than water sites, such as Firmicutes (the phyla that encompasses Bacillus and Clostridium) and the primary producer Cyanobacteria.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data obtained by the authors.

claim: In sediments, Cyanobacteria are part of the microbial mats along with Chlorobi and Spirochaetes.
source: In sediments, Cyanobacteria are part of the microbial mats along with Chlorobi and Spirochaetes
evidence: This is based on sequencing data obtained by the authors.

claim: In the soil, Cyanobacteria are part of the microbial crusts where Acidobacteria also play an important role in nutrient cycling along with Nitrospira.
source: while in the soil, Cyanobacteria are part of the microbial crusts where Acidobacteria also play an important role in nutrient cycling along with Nitrospira (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on sequencing data and shown in Figure 3.

claim: In CCB many different lineages of bacteria along with Cyanobacteria have an important role in the acquisition of nitrogen in the valley, contributing to the unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry.
source: It is important to underline that in CCB many different lineages of bacteria along with Cyanobacteria (López-Lozano et al., 2012) have an important role in the acquisition of nitrogen in the valley, contributing to the unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to López-Lozano et al., 2012.

claim: The diversity within the small scale in the Churince is immense, in particular when compared to 343 other studies based on 16S rRNA microbiomes.
source: The diversity within this small scale in the Churince is immense, in particular when compared to 343 other studies based also on 16S rRNA microbiomes.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of diversity indices.

claim: CCB contains 60 phyla which are roughly 66.28% of known prokaryotic phyla.
source: Major phyla abundances in CCB is depicted in bar plots, only the most abundant phyla are shown, but there are 60 phyla present in CCB which are roughly 66.28% of known prokaryotic phyla, in a single location few meters away.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2.

claim: Proteobacteria is the most abundant phylum in CCB, followed by Bacteroidetes, and Actinobacteria.
source: Proteobacteria is the most abundant phylum, followed by Bacteroidetes, and Actinobacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2.

claim: Some phyla like Planctomycetes, Cyanobacteria, Acidobacteria, Chlorobi, and Firmicutes are more abundant in the sediment and soil-associated samples than in water columns.
source: Some phyla like Planctomycetes, Cyanobacteria, Acidobacteria, Chlorobi, and Firmicutes are more abundant in the sediment and soil-associated samples than in water columns.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2.

claim: The most diverse environments, according to Shannon's diversity index, are the aquatic sediments of different sites in the world.
source: The most diverse environments, according to Shannon's diversity index (Table 1S), are the aquatic sediments of different sites in the world
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of diversity indices.

claim: The Churince's sediment had the highest Shannon value among the samples analyzed.
source: accordingly, in our dataset the Churince's sediment had the highest Shannon value.
evidence: This is based on diversity index calculations.

claim: Simpson's index showed that sediment was more diverse than water in Churince.
source: This was also supported by the Simpson's index that showed, as expected, that sediment was more diverse than water (Table 1S).
evidence: This is based on diversity index calculations.

claim: Both Shannon's and Simpson's diversity indices revealed a very high microbial diversity at Churince, even when compared with other microbial diversity hotspots, such as Pearl river in China, or Guerrero Negro in Mexico.
source: Even though most of the diversity at Churince had low abundance (Figure 2, see the size of the circles in the phylogenetic tree), both Shannon's and Simpson's diversity indices revealed a very high microbial diversity, even when compared with other microbial diversity hotspots, such as Pearl river in China, or Guerrero Negro in Mexico.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of diversity indices.

claim: From the collection of approximately 2500 cultured Bacillus spp. from CCB, 265 unique sequences were obtained at 97% identity.
source: From our collection of approximately 2500 cultured Bacillus spp. from CCB, 16S gene sequences were obtained and compared to sequences in databases. We obtained 265 unique sequences selected at 97% identity, a very conservative estimate for Bacillus.
evidence: This is based on sequencing and analysis of cultured strains.

claim: CCB strains formed multiple endemic lineages most of them with very deep branches in a global tree with 1019 other OTUs reported for Bacillus spp. from around the world.
source: In a global tree (Figure 4) with 1019 other OTUs reported for Bacillus spp. from around the world, we can observe the overall distribution and genetic distance of these CCB 16S sequences in relation to all known Bacillus lineages. We noticed that CCB strains formed multiple endemic (only found in CCB) lineages most of them with very deep branches
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The CCB sample increased by nearly 21% the number of previously known Bacillus.
source: and that our sample increased by nearly 21% the number of previously known Bacillus.
evidence: This is based on comparison with database sequences.

claim: Within the Bacillus spp. from CCB, two diverse sets of endemic lineages can be distinguished: one from sediment and another one closely related to marine Bacillus spp.
source: Within the Bacillus spp. from CCB, we can distinguish two diverse sets of endemic lineages: one from sediment and another one closely related to marine Bacillus spp. (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: CCB Bacillus spp. from sediments are significantly older than the marine related CCB lineages and may date back to the Ediacaran (635–541 mya, at the end of the Precambrian).
source: CCB Bacillus spp. from sediments are significantly older than the marine related CCB lineages, and according to our analyses calibrated using the divergence between the genus Bacillus and Geobacillus (Moreno-Letelier et al., 2012; Battistuzzi and Hedges, 2009) (Figure 5) may date back to the Ediacaran (635–541 mya, at the end of the Precambrian).
evidence: This is based on molecular clock analysis shown in Figure 5 and calibrated using citations.

claim: The Ediacaran period marks the start of the oxygenation of the ocean allowing not only the first animals to evolve but also the first aerobic Bacilli to diversify.
source: The Ediacaran period, marks the start of the oxygenation of the ocean allowing not only the first animals to evolve (Planavsky et al., 2010), but also the first aerobic Bacilli to diversify.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and a citation to Planavsky et al., 2010.

claim: CCB Bacillus species from water did not form a monophyletic group, which suggests independent synchronized origins dating to the late Jurassic.
source: Unlike the sediment lineage, CCB Bacillus species from water, did not form a monophyletic group, which suggests independent synchronized origins dating to the late Jurassic (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and molecular clock analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: A mixed representation of many lineages appears to have entered the CCB 'multidimensional niche bubble' simultaneously and did not become extinct.
source: A mixed representation of many lineages appears to have entered the CCB 'multidimensional niche bubble' simultaneously and did not become extinct.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic patterns.

claim: The presence of endemic and early divergent clades, with deep branches, of sediment and marine related CCB lineages, as well as the low extinction rates observed in these lineages, provides strong evidence for the lost world scenario.
source: The presence of endemic and early divergent clades, with deep branches, of sediment and marine related CCB lineages, as well as the low extinction rates observed in these lineages (Figure 7), provides strong evidence for the lost world scenario (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and diversification rate analyses shown in Figures 1D and 7.

claim: Speciation rates lower over time in soil and sediment Bacillus, while extinction rates remain constant.
source: Speciation rates lower over time, while extinction rates remain constant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The first pulse of marine migration at CCB can be explained by the abrupt change of nutrient stoichiometry balance at the end of the Ediacaran.
source: We think that the first pulse can be explained by the abrupt change of nutrient stoichiometry balance at the end of the Ediacaran (Elser et al., 2006; Planavsky et al., 2010; Stüeken and Kipp, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Elser et al., 2006; Planavsky et al., 2010; Stüeken and Kipp, 2017.

claim: The second pulse of marine migration may be explained by tectonics, as CCB is the point where the birth of the Tethys sea occurred in the western point of Pangea breakage.
source: However, the second pulse is more puzzling since it implies the migration of many independent lineages into the CCB shore. It is possible that the reason is tectonics, as CCB is the point where the birth of the Tethys sea occurred in the western point of Pangea breakage (Wolaver et al., 2013; Souza et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Wolaver et al., 2013 and Souza et al., 2006.

claim: None of the other lineages of Bacillus endemic to CCB have been reported at any other site.
source: Even though none of the other lineages of Bacillus endemic to CCB have been reported at any other site
evidence: This is based on comparison with database sequences.

claim: Other endemic lineages of Bacillus at CCB seem to constitute punctuated events of arrival to the 'island-like' niche and to have subsequently diversified locally.
source: they seem to constitute punctuated events of arrival to the 'island-like' niche and to have subsequently diversified locally.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic patterns.

claim: In a study of Bacillus spp. from diverse environments in India many cosmopolitan Bacillus spp. were collected that had short branches to sister species.
source: In contrast, in a study of Bacillus spp. from diverse environments in India many cosmopolitan Bacillus spp. were collected that had short branches to sister species (Yadav et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yadav et al., 2015.

claim: A much smaller sample of anaerobic Clostridiales and Bacteroidetes strains from CCB were fewer and did not form monophyletic groups endemic to CCB, even though some of their branches were early divergent.
source: When we compared the Bacillus sample with a much smaller sample of anaerobic Clostridiales and Bacteroidetes strains, the later were fewer and did not form monophyletic groups endemic to CCB, even though some of their branches were early divergent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Environmental conditions are known barriers to dispersal.
source: Environmental conditions are known barriers to dispersal.
evidence: This is based on established ecological knowledge.

claim: The extreme unbalanced nutrient stoichiometries at CCB could constrain immigration from phosphorus demanding populations that require a proportion of nitrogen to phosphorus closer to 16:1 for their survival.
source: The extreme unbalanced nutrient stoichiometries at CCB could certainly constrain immigration from phosphorus demanding populations that require a proportion of nitrogen to phosphorus closer to 16:1 (Elser et al., 2006) for their survival.
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Elser et al., 2006.

claim: Patagonia's isolated and oligotrophic lakes have unique microbial communities with low diversity.
source: This is the case of Patagonia's isolated and oligotrophic lakes with unique microbial communities with low diversity (Aguayo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Aguayo et al., 2017.

claim: CCB microbial populations are not only unique, they are also very diverse, despite CCB having an extremely unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry.
source: CCB microbial populations are not only unique, they are also very diverse, despite CCB having an extremely unbalanced nutrient stoichiometry.
evidence: This is based on diversity analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The small and endangered Churince system in CCB contains 57 out of the 86 known Bacteria phyla, which is 66.3% of the recorded bacterial diversity at phylum level.
source: Our data showed that the small and endangered Churince system in CCB contains 57 out of the 86 known Bacteria phyla, which is 66.3% of the recorded bacterial diversity at phylum level (data from 342 analysed microbiomes, Table 2S).
evidence: This is based on sequencing data and comparative analysis.

claim: The bacterial diversity of CCB is only comparable to Pearl River in China, where 48 microbial phyla were found.
source: This diversity is only comparable to Pearl River in China (Wang et al., 2012), where 48 microbial phyla were found.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis and supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2012.

claim: The Pearl River is a highly productive environment that receives inputs from multiple sources in the 2,400 km extension of China's third largest river.
source: The Pearl River is a highly productive environment that receives inputs from multiple sources in the 2,400 km extension of China's third largest river.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about the Pearl River.

claim: Churince is a small hydrological system fed by a spring and extends 1 km at most.
source: In contrast, Churince is a small hydrological system fed by a spring and extends 1 km at most.
evidence: This is a direct observation by the authors.

claim: Red Queen evolutionary processes have been shown to cause highly localized adaptation in numerous systems, including microbial ones.
source: Red Queen evolutionary processes have been shown to cause highly localized adaptation in numerous systems, including microbial ones.
evidence: This is based on established evolutionary theory.

claim: The Red Queen process proposes that organisms continuously adapt to changing conditions, particularly those involving antagonistic interactions within and between species, causing an increase in localized adaptation and coevolution.
source: The Red Queen process proposes that organisms continuously adapt to changing conditions, particularly those involving antagonistic interactions within and between species, causing an increase in localized adaptation and coevolution (Lawrence et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lawrence et al., 2012.

claim: Experiments of competition between strains of Bacillus from different sites within Churince showed marked antagonisms against different strains even from sites a few meters away, consistent with the Red Queen model.
source: Experiments of competition between strains of Bacillus from different sites within Churince showed marked antagonisms against different strains even from sites a few meters away (Pérez-Gutiérrez et al., 2013), consistent with the Red Queen model.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pérez-Gutiérrez et al., 2013.

claim: Extreme antagonism has been observed in the case of CCB Actinobacteria with non-CCB bacteria, which may prevent migration from bacteria outside the basin.
source: We have also observed extreme antagonism in the case of CCB Actinobacteria with non-CCB bacteria (Arocha-Garza et al., 2017), which may prevent migration from bacteria outside the basin.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arocha-Garza et al., 2017.

claim: Most of the bacterial lineages at CCB are local and clonal.
source: Indeed, we have observed that most of the bacterial lineages are local and clonal (Cerritos et al., 2011; Avitia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cerritos et al., 2011 and Avitia et al., 2014.

claim: CCB bacterial genomes are small and have few imprints of horizontal gene transfer (HGT).
source: Genomes are small and have few imprints of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) (Alcaraz et al., 2008; Alcaraz et al., 2010; Gómez-Lunar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alcaraz et al., 2008; Alcaraz et al., 2010; Gómez-Lunar et al., 2016.

claim: Vibrio from CCB thrives in perturbed, higher nutrient environments within the basin and displays recombination rates similar to those observed in marine Vibrio.
source: The only exception is Vibrio from CCB, a lineage that thrives in perturbed, higher nutrient environments within the basin, and that display recombination rates similar to the ones observed in marine Vibrio.
evidence: This is based on genomic analyses.

claim: Recombination in CCB Vibrio is mostly homologous, maintaining local adaptation and genetic isolation.
source: The caveats being, that such recombination is mostly homologous, maintaining local adaptation and genetic isolation (Gómez-Lunar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gómez-Lunar et al., 2018.

claim: Even though most CCB lineages are clonal, the rare HGT events allow linkage disequilibrium to break.
source: Even though most CCB lineages are clonal, the rare HGT events allow linkage disequilibrium to break.
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic data.

claim: Small population sizes or genetic sweeps as expected in completely clonal lineages are not observed in CCB.
source: Hence, we do not see small populations sizes or genetic sweeps as expected in completely clonal lineages (Cohan, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Cohan, 2016.

claim: Extinction rates are low, while diversification rates are high in some lineages at certain times at CCB.
source: Moreover, extinction rates are low, while diversification rates are high in some lineages at certain times (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on diversification rate analyses shown in Figure 7.

claim: Selective sweeps have not purged the genetic diversity that would drive lineages to extinction at CCB.
source: We believe that selective sweeps have not purged the genetic diversity that would drive lineages to extinction
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic diversity observations.

claim: Black Queen dynamics, in addition to Red Queen processes, are involved in maintaining diversity at CCB.
source: and involves Black Queen dynamics, in addition to the Red Queen processes discussed above.
evidence: This is an inference based on metabolic dependency observations.

claim: Tolerance and cooperation between strains are observed at CCB.
source: Tolerance and cooperation between strains are observed.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Strains of endemic lineages of Bacillus from Churince require cross feeding and cooperation to obtain even amino-acids.
source: For instance, strains of endemic lineages of Bacillus from Churince require cross feeding and cooperation to obtain even amino-acids (Rodríguez-Torres et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rodríguez-Torres et al., 2017.

claim: These cross-feeding observations fit a 'Black Queen' model where adaptation to severely limited resources lead to genomic streamlining and metabolic co-dependency.
